nameStory: The stinky squid gets its memorable name from its truly awful smell and its bizarre appearance. When mature, this fungus looks like an alien squid standing upright, with three or four thick 'arms' that curve up and connect at the top, forming a cage-like structure. The 'stinky' part becomes obvious the moment you get close - it produces one of the most foul odors in the fungal world!
description: The stinky squid is one of New England's most unusual fungi, belonging to a group called stinkhorns that are famous for their bizarre shapes and terrible smells. It starts as a whitish egg-like structure buried in soil or mulch, then erupts into a hollow, cage-like form with thick, fleshy arms that curve upward. The inside surfaces of these arms are coated with a dark greenish, slimy substance that produces an incredibly foul odor resembling rotting meat. This strange fungus can reach several inches tall and wide when fully expanded.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Produces an unmistakable, nauseating odor like rotting meat or sewage that can be detected from several feet away - this is the most reliable identifying feature

idTips.label: Structure
idTips.description: Forms a hollow cage with 3-4 thick, fleshy arms that curve upward and connect at the top, creating a distinctive squid-like or latticed appearance

idTips.label: Slime Layer
idTips.description: Dark greenish-black, sticky slime (called gleba) coats the inner surfaces of the arms and is the source of the horrible smell

idTips.label: Egg Stage
idTips.description: Begins as a whitish to pale brown, round egg-like structure about golf ball sized, often partially buried in soil

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Arms feel spongy and hollow when gently squeezed, with a somewhat rubbery texture similar to a mushroom stem

habitat: Look for stinky squids in rich, organic soil around gardens, compost areas, mulched flower beds, and wooded areas with lots of decaying plant matter. They particularly favor disturbed soils with plenty of organic matter like wood chips, leaf litter, or compost. In New England, they're often found near human habitation - in parks, gardens, and suburban areas rather than deep wilderness.

seasonality.spring: Egg stage may begin forming in late spring in warm, moist soil. Look for small, round, whitish bumps emerging from mulch or rich earth.
seasonality.summer: Peak fruiting season when mature cage-like forms appear, especially after warm rain. The terrible smell is strongest in hot, humid weather.
seasonality.fall: Can continue fruiting into early fall if conditions remain warm and moist. Late season specimens may be less smelly as the gleba washes away.
seasonality.winter: Not active in New England winters - completely dormant until soil warms again.

funFact: The stinky squid's horrible smell is actually a brilliant evolutionary strategy - it perfectly mimics rotting meat to trick flies and beetles into thinking they've found a feast, and these insects unknowingly become the fungus's personal spore delivery service!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other stinkhorn species like the red cage fungus (Clathrus ruber), but the stinky squid's arms always connect at the top forming a closed cage, while red cage fungi form an open lattice. Remember: if it looks like a closed squid with connected arms and smells like death, it's probably a stinky squid!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a stinkhorn, this species belongs to the cage fungi family (Clathraceae) rather than the true stinkhorn family, though both are closely related and share the strategy of using foul odors to attract insects. Many people mistake them for something that crawled out of the ocean due to their squid-like appearance.
compareHints: The stinky squid is the only member of its genus Pseudocolus found in New England, making it unique among our local fungi. Compared to other cage fungi in the region, it's distinguished by having fewer arms (3-4) that always connect at the top, creating a more squid-like appearance rather than the complex lattice patterns seen in related species. Its arms are also notably thicker and more substantial than those of other cage fungi.
